hints: Think about where ionic character is strongest in Period 3, at the left hand side with metals of low electronegativity bonded to chlorine.
walkthrough:
Locate the most metallic elements**
Picture Period 3 from left to right. Sodium and magnesium are strongly metallic with low electronegativity, so they transfer electrons to chlorine to form $\text{Na}^{+}$, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions packed in a giant ionic lattice.
Final answer: $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{MgCl}_{2}$

hints: Recall which Period 3 chlorides are covalent and hydrolyse completely to release $\text{HCl}$ and give a strongly acidic solution with pH 0 to 2.
walkthrough:
Spot the covalent chlorides that hydrolyse**
$\text{AlCl}_{3}$, $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ and $\text{PCl}_{5}$ are covalent. They react vigorously with water, breaking $\text{Al-Cl}$, $\text{Si-Cl}$ and $\text{P-Cl}$ bonds to form $\text{HCl}$ (aq), so the solution is strongly acidic.
Final answer: $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ and $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ and $\text{PCl}_{5}$

hints: Ask yourself which chloride simply dissolves into hydrated ions without reacting with water to produce $\text{H}^{+}$ or $\text{OH}^{-}$.
walkthrough:
Separate dissolving from reacting**
$\text{NaCl}$ is ionic and just dissociates into hydrated $\text{Na}^{+}$(aq) and $\text{Cl}^{-}$(aq). Neither ion hydrolyses, so no $\text{H}^{+}$ is produced and the solution stays neutral at pH 7. $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ gives a slightly acidic solution, so it does not count.

hints: Recall the melting point trend of the Period 3 elements themselves, which peaks at the giant covalent element in the middle of the period.
walkthrough:
Find the element with the highest melting point**
Across Na to Ar, melting point rises to a maximum at silicon. Silicon has a giant covalent tetrahedral lattice with many strong covalent bonds to break, so it melts far higher than metals Na, Mg, Al or molecular $\text{P}_{4}$, $\text{S}_{8}$, $\text{Cl}_{2}$. Its chloride is therefore $\text{SiCl}_{4}$.

hints: Remember chlorine with cold dilute alkali disproportionates to oxidation states -1 and +1, so look for a $\text{Cl}$(+1) salt plus water alongside $\text{NaCl}$.
walkthrough:
Recognise disproportionation in cold alkali**
With cold aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, $\text{Cl}_{2}$ is both oxidised and reduced: $$\text{Cl}_{2} + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ $\text{Cl}$ goes from 0 to -1 in $\text{NaCl}$ and 0 to +1 in $\text{NaClO}$, with water also formed to balance H and O.
Final answer: $\text{NaClO}$ / sodium chlorate(I) / sodium hypochlorite and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

hints: Focus on what happens to the $\text{-OH}$ group when $\text{PCl}_{5}$ acts, the $\text{OH}$ is swapped for $\text{Cl}$.
walkthrough:
See the OH for Cl swap**
The $\text{-OH}$ group of the alcohol is replaced by $\text{-Cl}$ to give the chloroalkane plus $\text{POCl}_{3}$ and $\text{HCl}$. One group substitutes for another, so this is substitution.

hints: Write out butane-1,3-diol as a carbon chain and mark the two carbons bearing $\text{-OH}$, then replace each $\text{-OH}$ with $\text{-Cl}$ because $\text{PCl}_{5}$ is in excess.
walkthrough:
Convert both OH groups**
Butane-1,3-diol is $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{3}$. With excess $\text{PCl}_{5}$ both alcohol groups react: $$\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{3} \rightarrow \text{ClCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHClCH}_{3}$$ Draw four carbons in a row, with $\text{Cl}$ replacing each $\text{OH}$, giving $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-CHCl-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ fully displayed.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHClCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ / 1,3-dichlorobutane, shown as displayed structure with all bonds and Cl atoms on C1 and C3

hints: Use the physical state clue, a liquid at room temperature with low melting point points to weak intermolecular forces rather than a giant lattice.
Use the chemical clue, vigorous reaction with water to give acid is characteristic of covalent chlorides, not ionic chlorides that simply dissolve.
walkthrough:
Read structure from melting point**
A cherry red liquid must have a low melting and boiling point. That tells you only weak van der Waals forces hold the particles together, so $\text{SCl}_{2}$ is simple molecular, not giant ionic or giant covalent.

Read bonding from reaction with water**
Ionic chlorides like $\text{NaCl}$ just dissolve. Covalent chlorides hydrolyse to release $\text{HCl}$. Because $\text{SCl}_{2}$ reacts vigorously with water to form an acidic solution, its bonding must be covalent.

Final answer: Structure: simple / molecular, as it has a low melting / boiling point (liquid).
Bonding: covalent, as it is hydrolysed by water to give an acidic solution.

hints: Combine the two given equations so that $\text{S}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}$ cancels, try adding reaction 1 to 4 x reaction 2 to make $\text{SCl}_{2}$ as the only product.
Remember to scale the enthalpy values in the same way and then divide by the number of moles of $\text{SCl}_{2}$ formed to get $\Delta H_{f}$ per mole.
walkthrough:
Build the Hess cycle to make $\text{SCl}_{2}$**
Target formation: $\frac{1}{8}\text{S}_{8}(\text{s}) + \text{Cl}_{2}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{SCl}_{2}(\text{l})$. Add reaction 1 to 4 lots of reaction 2 so $\text{S}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}$ cancels: $$\text{S}_{8} + 4\text{Cl}_{2} \rightarrow 4\text{S}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}$$ $$4\text{S}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2} + 4\text{Cl}_{2} \rightarrow 8\text{SCl}_{2}$$ Overall: $\text{S}_{8} + 8\text{Cl}_{2} \rightarrow 8\text{SCl}_{2}$.

Scale enthalpies and divide**
Total enthalpy = $-58.2 + 4(-40.6) = -58.2 -162.4 = -220.6\ \text{kJ}$ for 8 moles. Hence: $$\Delta H_{f} = \frac{-220.6}{8} = -27.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Final answer: $\Delta H_{f} = -27.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Count moles of gas on each side of reaction 2, ignoring liquids, and recall equilibrium shifts to the side with more gas moles when pressure falls.
walkthrough:
Count gases and apply Le Chatelier**
In reaction 2, $\text{S}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}(\text{l}) + \text{Cl}_{2}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SCl}_{2}(\text{l})$, there is 1 mole of gas on the left and 0 on the right. Decreasing pressure favours the side with more gas molecules to raise pressure, so the position shifts left.
Final answer: Equilibrium moves to the left, as there are more moles of gas on the left hand side.

hints: Start by stating what isomers must share, the same atoms in total.
Then state what must differ for them to be structural isomers, the order the atoms are joined together.
walkthrough:
State the same part**
Isomers I and II both have formula $\text{S}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}$, so structural isomers must first have the same molecular formula, meaning the same number of each type of atom.

State the different part**
They differ because the atoms are joined in a different order. Isomer I is $\text{Cl-S-S-Cl}$ while isomer II has both Cl atoms on one S with an $\text{S=S}$ bond, so they have different structural formulae.
Final answer: Molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae / different arrangement / connectivity of atoms.

hints: Count electron pairs around the S atom bonded to Cl and S in isomer I to find its electron pair geometry.
Recall how two lone pairs compress the tetrahedral angle of $109.5^{\circ}$ and what lower limit is sensible for a bent S atom.
walkthrough:
Assign the electron pairs on sulfur**
In isomer I, $\text{Cl-S-S-Cl}$, each S forms two single bonds (to Cl and to S) and carries two lone pairs to complete its octet. That is 4 electron pairs in total, based on a tetrahedron.

Apply lone pair repulsion**
Lone pair to lone pair repulsion is strongest and squeezes the bonding pairs together. So the $\text{Cl-S-S}$ angle is pushed below the tetrahedral $109.5^{\circ}$, typically to around $103^{\circ}$, but well above $90^{\circ}$. Any value between $90^{\circ}$ and $108^{\circ}$ is accepted.

Final answer: Bond angle $90^{\circ} < \text{Cl-S-S} \le 108^{\circ}$ (e.g. about $103^{\circ}$).
Each S has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs; lone pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair repulsion, compressing the angle below $109.5^{\circ}$.

hints: Draw the skeleton $\text{Cl}_{2}\text{S=S}$ and share two pairs between the two S atoms for the double bond and one pair with each Cl.
Complete the octets by adding the correct number of non bonding electrons on each Cl and each S, using dots for one atom and crosses for the other.
walkthrough:
Show the shared pairs**
Place central S bonded to two Cl atoms by single bonds and double bonded to the second S. Use dots for S and Cl electrons and crosses for the partner, so the $\text{S=S}$ shows 4 electrons in the overlap region and each $\text{S-Cl}$ shows 2 electrons.

Complete all lone pairs**
Give each Cl 6 non bonding electrons (3 lone pairs) to make 8 around Cl. Give the central S one lone pair and the terminal $\text{S}$ two lone pairs, so both S atoms also have full octets. Show outer shell electrons only.

Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram for $\text{Cl}_{2}\text{S=S}$ showing: S=S double bond (4 shared electrons), two S-Cl single bonds, each Cl with 3 lone pairs, lower S with 1 lone pair, upper S with 2 lone pairs; all outer shell electrons shown with dots and crosses to distinguish origin.
